title: A Ledger for the Autopsy
premise: Emrys Sterling, the reclusive coroner of Hollow Creek, is called to examine a drowned woman wearing clothes stolen from her own closet—a stranger with Emrys's face. The victim, it emerges, is Emrys's twin sister, given away at birth thirty years ago in a desperate bargain their dying mother struck to save one child. As Emrys investigates, she uncovers a decades-old cover-up involving the town's founding family, whose patriarch traded the infant for land deeds and silence. The killer is the family's aging fixer, silencing anyone who might expose the original crime, and Emrys herself is next on his list. In the end, Emrys chooses to publish the truth over protecting her own anonymity, closing the ledger at last—at the cost of the invisible life she built.
about_author: A. M. Nakamura is the pen name of a former rural registrar who spent a decade cataloguing deaths and disappearances in small-town archives before turning to fiction. They write quiet, forensic mysteries about people who thought they had escaped their pasts.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Emrys's POV. A fisherman drags a body from Miller's Pond at dawn; Emrys is summoned and notes the woman's face is unsettlingly familiar. She performs the preliminary exam alone, unsettled by a birthmark matching her own. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional calm.

chapters.title: Clothes That Fit
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Cataloguing the victim's effects, Emrys recognizes her own gray cardigan and boots—items from her locked closet. She tells no one, photographing everything first. Deputy Hale questions her routine. Emotional beat: the violation of being seen without consent.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Emrys walks the cemetery at dusk, grounding ritual interrupted by the realization she cannot place the victim among her dead. Flashback to why she came to Hollow Creek: to be no one's daughter, no one's twin. Emotional beat: loneliness as armor beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Witness
chapters.summary: POV shift to Maren Voss, retired schoolteacher and sole witness to something on the pond road the night of the death. Maren saw a truck with county plates but told police only about fog. Emotional beat: guilt compounding into fear as she reads the victim's description in the paper.

chapters.title: Jane Doe, Known
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Dental records arrive: the victim is Liora Sterling—born the same day as Emrys, same mother. Emrys sits with the file all night, unable to sign it. Emotional beat: grief for a sister she never knew existed.

chapters.title: What Mother Buried
chapters.summary: Emrys searches her late mother's belongings and finds a hospital bracelet, a second birth certificate with a different surname, and a letter begun and abandoned thirty years ago. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as betrayal.

chapters.title: The Bargain
chapters.summary: Maren POV. Maren remembers 1994: young Edith Sterling begging Aldous Crane, the town's patriarch, for help with medical bills—and what Aldous demanded in return. Maren kept silent then. Emotional beat: complicity curdling into terror that history is repeating.

chapters.title: Alibi, Thirty Years Old
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. She interviews Aldous Crane, now frail but sharp, who offers an airtight account of the night Liora arrived in town three weeks ago. He mentions, unprompted, that twins 'run unlucky.' Emotional beat: the hunter realizing she is also prey.

chapters.title: Three Weeks Earlier
chapters.summary: Reconstructed via Liora's recovered journal (Emrys POV reading). Liora traced her adoption, found Hollow Creek, and wrote of watching Emrys from across the street, unable to approach. Emotional beat: mirrored longing, unbearable tenderness.

chapters.title: The Locked Closet
chapters.summary: Emrys discovers how Liora entered her house: through a window Liora must have studied for days. Nothing else taken. She reports the theft minimally, protecting the investigation she now runs alone. Emotional beat: shame at resenting the dead.

chapters.title: Deputy Hale's Doubts
chapters.summary: Hale POV. The deputy notices discrepancies—the coroner's personal connection, the missing report on the clothing—and begins quietly pulling old files, including a 1994 drowning ruled accidental. Emotional beat: duty versus loyalty to a colleague he respects.

chapters.title: Miller's Pond, Drained
chapters.summary: Emrys orders the pond dragged. Divers recover a satchel: Liora's research, adoption papers, and photographs of Aldous Crane meeting someone at the boathouse—recently. Emotional beat: the case shifting from tragedy to conspiracy.

chapters.title: The Boathouse Meeting
chapters.summary: Maren POV. Maren identifies the second figure in the photos: Silas Renner, the Crane family's lawyer and fixer, the man who handled 'the arrangement' in 1994. She burns her own copy of an old letter, then regrets it. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid in installments.

chapters.title: Silas Renner, Esquire
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Renner receives her with impeccable courtesy, answers nothing, and warns her that reopening old matters 'serves no one, least of all the dead.' He knows her name before she gives it. Emotional beat: cold recognition of a professional adversary.

chapters.title: Land Deeds and Silence
chapters.summary: Hale POV. County records show the Crane fortune consolidated in 1994 through transfers signed by Edith Sterling—signatures Emrys confirms are forged. The motive for the original crime takes shape. Emotional beat: righteous anger hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: A Second Letter
chapters.summary: Emrys finds the finished version of her mother's letter hidden in the funeral home's oldest register: a full confession naming Aldous Crane and asking forgiveness of whichever daughter read it. Emotional beat: posthumous absolution, refused and needed at once.

chapters.title: Threats, Politely Worded
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. An anonymous note advises her to rule the death accidental. Her brakes fail on the pond road; she survives because she never trusts them. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into defiance.

chapters.title: Maren Comes Forward
chapters.summary: Maren POV. Terrified by the brake incident, Maren nearly flees town, then instead walks into Emrys's office and tells her about 1994—the bargain, the forged signatures, the baby traded for the deed. Emotional beat: two keepers of secrets finally sharing the weight.

chapters.title: The Other Twin
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Piecing together Liora's last weeks: she met Renner, showed him the evidence, and was bought off—or believed she was. A cashier's check stub in Liora's effects suggests a payment never collected. Emotional beat: hope that Liora died for refusing to be bought.

chapters.title: Accident, Ruled
chapters.summary: Under pressure from the county board, Emrys is forced to sign a preliminary ruling of accidental drowning while her toxicology remains 'pending.' She signs and immediately begins building the real case off the books. Emotional beat: the cost of staying employed versus staying honest.

chapters.title: Night Visitor
chapters.summary: Hale POV. Someone searches Emrys's office; Hale interrupts and is struck from behind, waking to find the 1994 file gone. He tells Emrys nothing, ashamed, and starts his own parallel inquiry. Emotional beat: guilt driving a reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: The Nurse Who Remembered
chapters.summary: Emrys tracks down Ruth Ibbetson, a retired delivery nurse, who recalls two infants, one healthy transfer arranged overnight, and a doctor paid to falsify records. The doctor, she says, still lives nearby. Emotional beat: memory as the last uncorruptible witness.

chapters.title: Dr. Fenn
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Dr. Fenn, dying and unafraid, confirms everything and adds the detail that matters: Aldous Crane didn't want a child—he wanted leverage over Edith Sterling, and got both. Emotional beat: the banality of cruelty.

chapters.title: Leverage
chapters.summary: Maren POV. Maren explains the deeper history: Edith discovered Crane's father's crimes—drownings, in fact—and the trade was hush money wearing a human face. Liora had found those same records. Emotional beat: generational rot made explicit.

chapters.title: Toxicology Returns
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. The delayed tox screen shows sedatives consistent with the drug used on Edith Sterling in 1994—same compound, same supplier trail. Homicide confirmed, and the pattern points to whoever has access to Crane's old stores: Renner. Emotional beat: vindication shadowed by danger.

chapters.title: Renner Moves
chapters.summary: Renner POV (first time inside his head, cool and procedural). He burns documents, arranges an 'accident' for Ruth Ibbetson, and notes that Emrys Sterling is a problem requiring elegance, not force. Emotional beat: chilling competence.

chapters.title: Ruth's House Burns
chapters.summary: Emrys arrives minutes after the fire; Ruth survives, barely, and whispers that Renner kept a ledger—literally—of every transaction, including 1994. Emotional beat: fury at the escalation, gratitude sharpening focus.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Hale POV. Following Ruth's hint, Hale finds the ledger hidden in the cemetery's receiving vault—Renner's habit of hiding things where only the coroner looks. It records payments, silences, and one final entry scheduled: 'E.S., settlement pending.' Emotional beat: horror and proof in one binding.

chapters.title: Settlement Pending
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. She realizes 'settlement' means her death, timed to close the estate as Aldous Crane enters hospice. She has perhaps four days. She chooses not to run. Emotional beat: the invisible woman deciding to be seen.

chapters.title: Going Public
chapters.summary: Emrys hands copies of the ledger to the state police, a journalist, and Maren—redundancy as protection. Renner's elegant options narrow. Emotional beat: courage as arithmetic.

chapters.title: Crane's Deathbed
chapters.summary: Emrys visits Aldous Crane, who neither confesses nor denies, but says: 'Your mother understood that some children are the price of a town.' Emrys tells him his empire ends this week. Emotional beat: confrontation without catharsis.

chapters.title: The Trap at the Pond
chapters.summary: Emrys lets herself appear alone at Miller's Pond at night, feeding Renner the opportunity he needs. Hale and state troopers hold the treeline. Emotional beat: terror managed like an autopsy—methodical, cold.

chapters.title: Renner's Confession
chapters.summary: Renner, caught between exposure and loyalty, comes to finish it personally and talks as he works—thirty years of cleaning up for Cranes, including Liora, who begged and then spat at him. Troopers move in. Emotional beat: evil as bureaucracy, finally named.

chapters.title: Arrest
chapters.summary: Hale POV. The arrest is quiet, almost anticlimactic; Renner requests his lawyer and glances at Emrys with something like respect. The ledger enters evidence. Emotional beat: justice arriving without fanfare, which is its own kind of wound.

chapters.title: What the Dead Are Owed
chapters.summary: Emrys amends the ruling: homicide, and formally names Liora Sterling. She plans a burial beside their mother. Emotional beat: grief finally permitted to do its work.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Stone
chapters.summary: The funeral draws half the town; Maren speaks, confessing her thirty-year silence publicly. Emrys stands exposed and unmoved by shame for the first time. Emotional beat: community as consequence and consolation.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Emrys opens the estate file: Liora left everything to 'my sister, if she exists.' A modest savings, the journal, and a note: 'I only wanted to see you once.' Emotional beat: love arriving too late and exactly on time.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Emrys considers leaving Hollow Creek, the old reflex, and unpacks instead—hanging Liora's photograph beside her mother's letter. She resigns nothing, hides nothing more. Emotional beat: identity chosen rather than endured.

chapters.title: Closing the Ledger
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Emrys POV. Months later, trials concluded, Emrys walks the cemetery naming every grave—including, now, two Sterlings under one stone. A new case arrives; she answers the door with the lights on. Emotional beat: peace earned, vigilance kept, invisibility voluntarily surrendered.
